title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident shows a failure in how AI training data is sourced and validated. An entity without legal existence or named staff published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days, structured to mimic user queries and designed to optimize for ingestion by AI chatbots. The reports presented arguable political positions as neutral research, using heavy citation of a single study to create an appearance of authority. A system that draws training data from published research with minimal verification of source credibility would absorb this content as though it were legitimate scholarship.

The failure occurred upstream of any deployed chatbot, in the ecosystem of information that AI systems train on. Catching this would have required verification that the Hanover Institute exists as a legal entity with named staff and an independent publication record, rather than accepting it as a credible source based on the polish and volume of its output alone. The operation was financed by a foreign government through intermediaries, a fact that would not be apparent from the content itself.

It is not established whether any major AI system actually incorporated these reports into its training data or was materially affected by the campaign.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

An Israeli-funded fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute published over 560,000 words across 124 reports in nine days using a platform designed to optimize content for artificial intelligence chatbots. The institute, which does not exist as a legal entity and has no named staff, presented pro-Israel arguments on controversial topics including genocide allegations and war crimes as neutral research. A New York media company filed the operation with the US Justice Department under foreign agent registration requirements, revealing that the broader campaign is financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government through intermediaries including the European advertising group Havas Media.

The operation is part of a larger effort to influence how AI systems respond to questions about Israel. The Guardian's analysis found the reports were structured like questions users might ask chatbots and heavily cited a single study on antisemitism to frame discussions. Israeli officials have expressed doubts about the campaign's effectiveness, with some calling it a waste of money as American public opinion has shifted significantly against Israel, with only 36 percent of Americans sympathizing with Israel in recent polling compared to higher levels in previous years.
